label: Phaedo · Two Objections
title: Two Objections
paragraphs: When Socrates had said this there was silence for a long time. Socrates himself was deep in the argument that had been made, as one could see by looking at him, and so were most of us. But Cebes and Simmias were talking a little with each other. Socrates saw the two of them and questioned them. What is it? he said. Surely you do not think that what has been said falls short? It certainly still leaves many doubts and many holds for an opponent, if anyone is going to go through it thoroughly. Now if the two of you are considering something else, I say nothing. But if you are in some difficulty about these things, do not hesitate to speak yourselves and go through it, if it appears to you that it could have been said better in some way, and to take me along with you too, if you think you will find your way more easily with me.

And Simmias said: Well, Socrates, I will tell you the truth. For some time now each of us, being in difficulty, has been pushing the other forward and telling him to ask, because we want to hear, but hesitate to give trouble, for fear it may be unpleasant for you in your present misfortune.

When he heard this he laughed gently and said: Good heavens, Simmias. I would surely have a hard time persuading other people that I do not consider my present fortune a misfortune, when I cannot persuade even you, and you are afraid that I am in a more difficult temper now than in my earlier life. And, it seems, you think I am poorer at prophecy than the swans. When they perceive that they must die, though they sang in the time before as well, they then sing most and most beautifully, rejoicing that they are about to go away to the god whose servants they are. But human beings, because of their own fear of death, tell lies about the swans too, and say that they are lamenting their death and sing out from grief. They do not reckon that no bird sings when it is hungry or cold or suffering any other pain, not even the nightingale herself, or the swallow, or the hoopoe, which they say sing in lament from grief. But it does not appear to me that these sing in grief, or the swans either. Rather, I think, because they belong to Apollo they are prophetic, and they sing because they know beforehand the good things in Hades, and they are glad on that day beyond any time before.

And I consider that I myself am a fellow slave of the swans and sacred to the same god, and that I have the gift of prophecy from our master no less than they do, and that I am leaving life no more downhearted than they. No, as far as that goes, you must speak and ask whatever you wish, for as long as the Eleven of Athens allow it.

Well said, said Simmias. I will tell you what my difficulty is, and then he will tell you in what way he does not accept what has been said. For I think, Socrates, as perhaps you do too, that to know the plain truth about such things in this present life is either impossible or something very hard; but that not to test what is said about them in every way, and to give up before one is worn out with examining them from every side, is the mark of a very soft man. For one must accomplish one of these things about them: either learn how it is, or find it out, or, if that is impossible, take the best of human arguments at least, and the hardest to refute, and riding on it as on a raft sail through life in danger — unless one could make the journey more safely and with less danger on a firmer vessel, some divine word. And so now I will not be ashamed to ask, since you yourself say this, and I will not blame myself at a later time for not having said now what I think. For to me, Socrates, when I examine what has been said, both by myself and with him, it does not quite appear to have been adequately said.
And Socrates said: Yes, my friend, perhaps what appears to you is true. But tell me in what way it was not adequate.

In this way, it seems to me, he said: one could give this same argument about an attunement too, and a lyre and its strings — that the attunement is something invisible and bodiless and altogether beautiful and divine in the tuned lyre, while the lyre itself and the strings are bodies and bodily and composite and earthy and akin to what is mortal. So when someone smashes the lyre, or cuts and snaps the strings, suppose a person insisted, by the same argument as yours, that that attunement must still exist and has not perished. For there would be no way, he would say, that the lyre should still exist when its strings have been snapped, and the strings too, which are of mortal kind, and yet the attunement have perished, which is of one nature and one family with the divine and immortal, perishing before the mortal. No, he would say, the attunement itself must still exist somewhere, and the wood and the strings will rot away before anything happens to it.

And in fact, Socrates, I think you yourself have had this in mind, that we take the soul to be something very much of this kind: our body being as it were strung and held together by hot and cold and dry and wet and things of that sort, our soul is a blending and an attunement of these very things, when they are blended well and in due measure with one another. If, then, the soul is in fact a kind of attunement, it is clear that when our body is slackened or tightened beyond measure by diseases and other evils, the soul must at once perish, most divine though it is, just like the other attunements, those in sounds and those in all the works of craftsmen, while the remains of each body last a long time, until they are burned or rot away. See, then, what we will say to this argument, if someone claims that the soul, being a blending of the things in the body, is the first to perish in what is called death.

Socrates looked straight at us, as he so often used to, and smiled. What Simmias says is fair, he said. So if any of you is more resourceful than I am, why does he not answer? For he looks like a man who has taken hold of the argument in no poor way. But I think that before the answer we should first hear from Cebes as well, what charge he in his turn brings against the argument, so that with the time gained we may consider what we will say; and then, when we have heard them, either agree with them, if they seem to sing in tune, or if not, then at that point plead for the argument. Come, Cebes, he said, speak. What was it that troubled you in your turn?

I will, said Cebes. To me the argument appears to be still in the same place, and to be open to the same charge we made before. That our soul existed even before it came into this form — I do not take back that this has been very neatly and, if it is not too much to say, very adequately proved. But that it still exists somewhere when we have died does not seem to me proved in the same way. That the soul is not stronger and longer-lasting than the body, I do not concede to Simmias' objection; for I think it is very far superior in all these respects. Why then, the argument might say, do you still disbelieve, when you see that after the person has died the weaker part still exists? Do you not think the longer-lasting part must still be kept safe during that time?

Consider, then, whether there is anything in what I say to this; for I too, it seems, need an image, as Simmias did. It seems to me that this is like someone giving this argument about an old weaver who has died: that the person has not perished but exists somewhere safe and sound, and he would offer as evidence the cloak the man was wearing, which he had woven himself, that it is sound and has not perished. And if anyone disbelieved him, he would ask which is the longer-lasting kind of thing, a human being or a cloak that is in use and being worn; and when someone answered that a human being lasts much longer, he would think it had been proved that then, beyond all doubt, the person is safe and sound, since the shorter-lived thing has not perished.

But I think, Simmias, that this is not so; consider what I am saying, you too. Anyone would take it that the man who says this is talking foolishly. For this weaver wore out many such cloaks and wove them, and he perished later than those, many as they were, but earlier, I suppose, than the last one; and a human being is not for that reason any the more inferior to a cloak, or weaker.

The soul in relation to the body would admit, I think, of this same image, and anyone who said these very things about them would seem to me to speak reasonably: that the soul is long-lasting, and the body weaker and shorter-lived. But, he would say, each of the souls wears out many bodies, especially if it lives many years. For if the body is in flux and perishing while the person is still alive, and yet the soul always weaves again what is being worn out, still it would be necessary that when the soul perished it should happen to be wearing its last piece of weaving, and should perish before that one alone; and when the soul had perished, then at last the body would show the weakness of its nature, and quickly rot and be gone.

So it is not yet right to trust this argument and be confident that when we die our soul still exists somewhere. For suppose someone granted to a person who says this even more than what you say, and allowed him not only that our souls existed in the time before we were born, but that nothing prevents the souls of some from still existing after we die, and going on existing, and being born many times and dying again — for the thing is by nature so strong that a soul holds out through being born many times. But suppose that, having allowed this, he would not go on to concede that it does not suffer in its many births, and does not at the end perish altogether in one of its deaths; and suppose he said that no one knows this death, this dissolution of the body which brings destruction to the soul — for it is impossible for any one of us to perceive it. If that is so, then no one who is confident in the face of death can be anything but foolishly confident, unless he is able to prove that the soul is altogether immortal and imperishable. Otherwise the one who is about to die must always fear for his own soul, that in this present unyoking from the body it may perish altogether.

When we heard them say this we were all put into an unpleasant state, as we told one another afterward, because we had been firmly persuaded by the earlier argument, and now they seemed to have thrown us into confusion again and cast us down into disbelief, not only toward the arguments already given but toward what was going to be said later as well: we feared that we were worth nothing as judges, or even that the things themselves could not be trusted.

ECHECRATES: By the gods, Phaedo, I do not blame you. For now that I have heard you, it comes over me to say something like this to myself: What argument will we trust now? How very persuasive the argument was that Socrates gave, and now it has fallen into disbelief. For this argument has a wonderful hold on me, now and always, that our soul is a kind of attunement, and when it was spoken it reminded me, as it were, that I too had held this view before. And I very much need some other argument, over again as if from the beginning, which will persuade me that when a person dies the soul does not die with him. So tell me, by Zeus, how Socrates went after the argument. And was he too, as you say you were, visibly distressed at all, or was he not, but came gently to the argument's aid? And did he aid it adequately, or did he fall short? Go through everything for us as exactly as you can.

PHAEDO: Well, Echecrates, I had often wondered at Socrates, but I never admired him more than when I was with him then. That he had something to say is perhaps nothing strange. But what I wondered at most in him was this: first, how pleasantly and kindly and admiringly he received the young men's argument; then how sharply he perceived what the arguments had done to us; and then how well he healed us, and called us back like men who had fled and been beaten, and turned us to follow along with him and examine the argument together.
ECHECRATES: How?

PHAEDO: I will tell you. I happened to be sitting at his right, beside the couch, on a low stool, and he on something much higher than mine. So he stroked my head and gathered up the hair on my neck in his hand — for it was his habit, now and then, to play with my hair — and said: Tomorrow, perhaps, Phaedo, you will cut off this beautiful hair.
So it seems, Socrates, I said.
Not if you take my advice.
What then? I said.

Today, he said, I will cut mine and you will cut this, if our argument dies and we cannot bring it back to life. And if I were you and the argument got away from me, I would swear an oath, as the Argives did, not to wear my hair long until I had fought again and beaten the argument of Simmias and Cebes.
But against two, I said, even Heracles is said to be no match.
Then call on me as your Iolaus, he said, while there is still light.
I call on you, then, I said, not as Heracles, but as Iolaus calling on Heracles.
It will make no difference, he said. But first let us be on our guard against a certain thing happening to us.
What kind of thing? I said.

That we do not become haters of argument, he said, as people become haters of people; for there is no greater evil that could happen to anyone, he said, than to have come to hate arguments. Hatred of argument and hatred of people come about in the same way. Hatred of people slips in from trusting someone very much without skill, and believing the person to be altogether true and sound and trustworthy, and then a little later finding him bad and untrustworthy, and then another again. And when this has happened to someone many times, and above all at the hands of those he would have thought his nearest and closest friends, in the end, after many such collisions, he hates everyone and believes there is nothing sound in anyone at all. Or have you never noticed this happening?
Certainly, I said.

Then is it not shameful, he said, and clear that such a person was trying to deal with people without skill in human things? For if he had dealt with them with skill, he would have thought as it really is: that the very good and the very bad are few, both of them, and those in between are the most.
What do you mean? I said.

It is the same, he said, as with the very small and the very large. Do you think anything is rarer than to find a very large or a very small person, or dog, or anything else? Or again one that is fast or slow, or ugly or beautiful, or white or black? Or have you not noticed that in all such things the extremes at either end are rare and few, and those in between are plentiful and many?
Certainly, I said.
Then do you think, he said, that if a contest in wickedness were held, there too those who came first would appear very few?
Likely enough, I said.

Yes, likely, he said. But it is not in this way that arguments are like people — I was only following where you led just now — but in that other way: when someone trusts that an argument is true, without skill in arguments, and then a little later it seems to him to be false, sometimes when it is and sometimes when it is not, and then another and another. And above all those who have spent their time on arguments for contradiction, you know, end by thinking they have become the wisest of people, and that they alone have understood that there is nothing sound or firm in any thing or in any argument, but that all the things that are simply turn up and down as in the Euripus, and stay in no place for any time.
Very much so, I said; that's true.

Then, Phaedo, he said, it would be a pitiful thing to happen, if there really is some true and firm argument that can be understood, and yet someone, through being in the company of arguments of the kind that seem true at one time and not at another, were not to blame himself or his own lack of skill, but in the end, because of his pain, were gladly to push the blame off himself onto the arguments, and from then on were to spend the rest of his life hating and abusing arguments, and be deprived of the truth and the knowledge of the things that are.
By Zeus, I said, pitiful indeed.

First, then, he said, let us be on our guard against this, and let us not admit into the soul the thought that there may be nothing sound in arguments, but much rather that we are not yet sound ourselves, and must be brave and strive to be sound — you and the others for the sake of your whole life to come, and I for the sake of death itself. For I am in danger, at this moment, of treating this very matter not as a lover of wisdom but, like the wholly uneducated, as a lover of victory. They too, when they dispute about something, do not care how the thing stands that the argument is about; what they strive for is that what they themselves have laid down shall seem so to those present. And I think that at this moment I will differ from them only this much: I will not strive to make what I say seem true to those present, except as a side matter, but to make it seem so as much as possible to me myself.

For I reckon, my dear friend — see how greedily — that if what I say is in fact true, it is a fine thing to be persuaded of it; and if there is nothing for one who has died, then at least for just this time before my death I will be less unpleasant to those present with lamenting. And this folly of mine will not last on with me — that would be an evil — but will perish a little later. So prepared, Simmias and Cebes, he said, I come to the argument. But you, if you take my advice, will give little thought to Socrates and much more to the truth: if I seem to you to say something true, agree with it; and if not, resist with every argument, taking care that I do not in my eagerness deceive both myself and you, and go off like a bee, leaving my sting behind.

But we must go on, he said. First remind me of what you were saying, if I appear not to remember. Simmias, I think, disbelieves and fears that the soul, though it is something more divine and more beautiful than the body, may still perish before it, being in the form of an attunement. And Cebes seemed to me to grant me this, that the soul is longer-lasting than the body, but to say that this is unclear to everyone: whether the soul, after wearing out many bodies many times, may now leave its last body and perish itself, and whether death may be just this, the destruction of the soul, since the body never stops perishing at all. Is it anything other than these things, Simmias and Cebes, that we must examine?
They both agreed that it was these.
Then do you reject all the earlier arguments, he said, or some and not others?
Some, they said, and not others.

Then what do you say, he said, about that argument in which we said that learning is recollection, and that, this being so, our soul must have existed somewhere else earlier, before it was bound in the body?
I was wonderfully persuaded by it then, said Cebes, and I stand by it now as by no other argument.
And I am the same myself, said Simmias, and I would be very surprised if I ever thought otherwise about this.

And Socrates said: But you must think otherwise, my friend from Thebes, if this belief stays, that an attunement is a composite thing, and that the soul is a kind of attunement composed of the things strung in the body. For surely you will not accept it even from yourself, if you say that an attunement existed, already composed, before the things existed from which it had to be put together. Or will you?
Not at all, Socrates, he said.

Do you see, then, he said, that this is what you turn out to be saying, when you say that the soul exists even before it comes into human form and body, and that it exists composed of things that do not yet exist? For an attunement is surely not like the thing you compare it to. The lyre and the strings and the notes come into being first, still untuned, and the attunement is put together last of all and perishes first. So how will this argument of yours sing in tune with that one?
Not at all, said Simmias.
And yet, he said, if any argument ought to be in tune, it is the one about attunement.
It ought, said Simmias.
Well, this one of yours is not in tune, he said. See, then, which of the two arguments you choose: that learning is recollection, or that the soul is an attunement?

The first, by far, Socrates, he said. For this other one came to me without proof, from a certain likelihood and fair appearance, which is why most people believe it too. But I am aware that arguments which make their proofs through likelihoods are impostors, and if one is not on guard against them they deceive one thoroughly, in geometry and in everything else. But the argument about recollection and learning has been given through a hypothesis worth accepting. For it was said, I think, that our soul exists even before it comes into a body, just as the being that bears the name of ‘what is’ belongs to it. And this I have accepted, as I persuade myself, adequately and rightly. So for these reasons I must, it seems, not accept it either from myself or from anyone else when it is said that the soul is an attunement.
And what about this, Simmias? he said. Do you think it belongs to an attunement, or to any other composition, to be in any other state than that of the things it is composed of?
Not at all.
Nor, I think, to do anything, or have anything done to it, other than what they do or have done to them?
He agreed.
Then it does not belong to an attunement to lead the things it is put together from, but to follow them.
He thought so too.
Then an attunement is far from being able to move or sound in opposition to its own parts, or oppose them in any other way.
Far indeed, he said.
Well then: is not each attunement by nature an attunement in just the way it has been tuned?
I don't understand, he said.

Is it not so, he said, that if it is tuned more and to a greater extent, supposing that can happen, it would be more an attunement and a greater one, and if less and to a smaller extent, less of one and a smaller one?
Certainly.
Now is this so of soul — that even in the smallest degree one soul is more and to a greater extent than another, or less and to a smaller extent, this very thing, a soul?
Not in any way whatever, he said.
Come then, by Zeus, he said. Is one soul said to have intelligence and virtue and to be good, and another to have folly and wickedness and to be bad? And is this said truly?
Truly indeed.

Then of those who lay it down that the soul is an attunement, what will any of them say these things are that are in souls, virtue and vice? Another attunement again, and a lack of attunement? And that the one soul, the good one, has been tuned, and has in itself, being an attunement, another attunement, while the other is untuned itself and has no other in it?
I cannot say, said Simmias. But clearly the one who laid that down would say something of the kind.

But it has already been agreed, he said, that one soul is no more and no less a soul than another; and this agreement is that one attunement is no more and to no greater extent, and no less and to no smaller extent, an attunement than another. Is that not so?
Certainly.
And that what is no more and no less an attunement has been tuned neither more nor less. Is that so?
It is.
And what has been tuned neither more nor less — does it share in attunement to any greater or smaller extent, or equally?
Equally.
Then a soul, since one is no more and no less than another this very thing, a soul, has not been tuned more or less either?
Just so.
And being in that condition, it could have no greater share in lack of attunement or in attunement?
No, it could not.
And again, being in that condition, could one soul have any greater share in vice or virtue than another, if vice is lack of attunement and virtue attunement?
None greater.

Or rather, Simmias, I suppose, by the correct argument no soul will share in vice, if it is an attunement. For an attunement, surely, being completely this very thing, an attunement, could never share in lack of attunement.
No indeed.
Nor, surely, could a soul, being completely a soul, share in vice.
How could it, from what has been said?
By this argument, then, we find that all souls of all living things will be equally good, if souls are by nature equally this very thing, souls.
I think so, Socrates, he said.
And do you think, he said, that this is well said, and that the argument would have come to this if the hypothesis were right, that the soul is an attunement?
Not in any way whatever, he said.
Well then, he said: of all the things in a human being, is there any you say rules other than the soul, especially a wise one?
No, I do not.

Does it rule by giving way to the feelings of the body, or by opposing them as well? I mean something like this: when heat and thirst are there, it pulls the opposite way, toward not drinking, and when hunger is there, toward not eating; and in countless other ways, I suppose, we see the soul opposing the things of the body. Or do we not?
Very much so.

And did we not agree earlier that, being an attunement, it could never sing a tune opposed to the tightening and slackening and plucking and whatever else is done to the things it is composed of, but would follow them and never lead?
We did agree, he said. Of course.

Well then: does it not now appear to us to be doing the complete opposite — leading all those things from which someone says it is composed, and opposing them in almost everything through the whole of life, and mastering them in every way, punishing some more harshly and with pain, in physical training and in medicine, and others more gently, now threatening and now warning, talking to the desires and angers and fears as one thing talking to another? It is just as Homer too has made it in the Odyssey, where he says of Odysseus: ‘He struck his chest and rebuked his own heart: Endure, my heart; you once endured something worse.’ Do you think he composed this with the thought that the soul is an attunement, and the kind of thing to be led by the feelings of the body, and not the kind to lead them and master them, being itself something far more divine than an attunement?
By Zeus, Socrates, I think so.
Then, my good friend, it is in no way right for us to say that the soul is a kind of attunement; for, it seems, we would agree neither with Homer, a divine poet, nor with ourselves.
That is so, he said.

divergences.phrase: ἡ μὲν ἁρμονία ἀόρατον καὶ ἀσώματον καὶ πάγκαλόν τι καὶ θεῖόν ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ἡρμοσμένῃ λύρᾳ
divergences.older: harmony is a thing invisible, incorporeal, perfect, divine, existing in the lyre which is harmonized
divergences.lectio: the attunement is something invisible and bodiless and altogether beautiful and divine in the tuned lyre
divergences.note: Harmonia is not chords sounding together, which Greek music did not have; it is the tuning of the strings, their being tightened and slackened into the right relation. The edition says attunement and tuned throughout, so that the reply at 92a–94e, where a tuning can be more or less a tuning and can never lead its strings, reads as an argument about the same thing.

divergences.phrase: μὴ γενώμεθα μισόλογοι, ὥσπερ οἱ μισάνθρωποι γιγνόμενοι
divergences.lectio: That we do not become haters of argument, he said, as people become haters of people
divergences.note: Jowett carries the Greek word over and then stops to define it, and his haters of ideas loses the logos that has been the subject all day. Plato coins the word in passing and lets the comparison explain it; the edition gives plain English for both hatreds and adds nothing.

divergences.phrase: ἐπὶ βεβαιοτέρου ὀχήματος, ἢ λόγου θείου τινός
divergences.lectio: a firmer vessel, some divine word
divergences.note: Simmias sets the best of human arguments against a logos that is divine, the same noun both times: an oracle, perhaps, or a teaching of the mysteries. There is no single God in the phrase, and he does not say that such a word has been given.
